questions.q: Why does this lesson use a simulated depolarizing noise model instead of a literal real-hardware job result?
options: Because depolarizing noise is identical to real hardware noise in every respect
Because simulated results are always more accurate than real ones
Because this environment cannot execute a real IBM Quantum job, so the lesson honestly approximates what a noisy run looks like instead
Because IBM hardware does not produce measurement counts
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit up front: it cannot run on real IBM hardware here, so it illustrates the kind of noise signature a real device would plausibly produce using a depolarizing-noise approximation, not an actual pulled result.

questions.q: For the ideal (noiseless) Bell-state circuit, what are the exact probabilities of each outcome?
options: All four outcomes equally likely at 0.25 each
questions.explain: The ideal, noiseless Bell-state circuit only ever produces 00 or 11, each with exact probability 0.5; 01 and 10 have exact probability 0 since no path through the ideal circuit produces a mismatched pair.

questions.q: Under the depolarizing noise model with p=0.05 applied to the entangling gate, what is the exact probability of outcome `01`?
questions.explain: The lesson gives the exact depolarizing-channel result for this noise level as P(01) = 0.0125 (and P(10) = 0.0125 as well), with the dominant P(00) and P(11) each reduced to 0.4875.

questions.q: A real seeded draw at shots=4096 from the noisy probabilities gave `{'00': 2005, '11': 2003, '01': 35, '10': 53}`. What is the correct interpretation of the nonzero `01`/`10` counts?
options: The expected signature of genuine gate and/or readout error on real hardware, not a circuit bug
A sign the simulator's random number generator is broken
Clear evidence of a bug in the circuit that must be fixed
Proof the qubits were never actually entangled
questions.explain: Seeing nonzero counts on outcomes that are exactly 0 under ideal math is the real diagnostic signature of hardware noise (gate error, readout error) — not a sign of a coding mistake, and expected on real devices.

questions.q: What is the practical next question to ask when you observe this kind of noise signature on real hardware, per this lesson?
options: Whether to switch to a different programming language
Whether to ignore the result entirely and discard the job
Whether to rewrite the circuit from scratch
Whether the noise level is consistent with the backend and small enough to be usable, or whether error mitigation is needed
questions.explain: The useful question isn't 'what did I do wrong' — it's whether the observed noise level is consistent with expectations for that backend and acceptable for your purposes, or whether you need error mitigation (the subject of Chapter 7) to clean it up.
